body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Weight reduction and owner-reported mobility in overweight dogs with osteoarthritis: a randomised trial in referral practice","authors":"Hallorann-Ueda P, Brightwell-Osei A, Fonseca-Lind M","year":2018,"venue":"Journal of Companion Animal Practice","doi":"10.5555/jcap.2018.0612","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Sixty-two overweight dogs with osteoarthritis at a referral hospital were randomly allocated to a supervised weight loss programme or to diet advice alone for 16 weeks. Dogs in the programme lost a median of 9.4 percent of body weight against 2.1 percent. Owner-reported mobility scores improved by a mean of 6.1 points on a 44-point index in the programme group and by 1.8 points with advice alone. Lameness assessed on a force plate improved in dogs that lost at least 6 percent of body weight. Owners were not blinded, and referral patients may be more motivated than first-opinion clients."},{"title":"Nurse-led weight clinics in first-opinion practice: attendance and weight outcomes in 1,240 dogs","authors":"Rasmussen-Adeyemi K, Tolliver-Chen J","year":2021,"venue":"Veterinary Nursing Evidence","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed attendance and weight records for 1,240 dogs enrolled in nurse-led weight clinics at 31 first-opinion practices. Only 38 percent of dogs attended for six months. Among dogs that completed six months, median weight loss was 8.1 percent, and 44 percent lost at least 10 percent of their starting weight. Dogs whose owners received a phone call between visits were more likely to keep attending. Outcomes for dogs that stopped attending were unknown, so average weight loss across all enrolled dogs could not be estimated."},{"title":"Validation of an owner-completed mobility and comfort index for dogs with chronic joint pain","authors":"Ogunleye-Harper S, Vitale-Kristensen E, Moss-Achebe D","year":2016,"venue":"Veterinary Clinical Outcomes Journal","doi":"10.5555/vcoj.2016.0231","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We evaluated an 11-item owner-completed index of mobility and comfort, scored 0 to 44 with higher scores meaning worse, in 212 dogs with chronic joint pain and 80 healthy dogs. Internal consistency was 0.91 and test-retest reliability over one week was 0.88. Scores were higher in dogs with more severe radiographic osteoarthritis and fell after pain relief was started. Owners' judgements of meaningful change corresponded to a difference of about 4 points. The standard deviation of change scores was 8 points. The index was validated with English-speaking owners only."},{"title":"Activity monitor counts versus owner-reported mobility in dogs with osteoarthritis","authors":"Petrakis-Nwosu L, Glenister-Arai T","year":2020,"venue":"Veterinary Clinical Outcomes Journal","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Forty-eight dogs with osteoarthritis wore a collar-mounted activity monitor for two weeks before and after the start of pain relief, while their owners completed a mobility index. Changes in activity counts correlated only moderately with changes in owner scores (correlation 0.41). When dogs received an inactive tablet during a blinded phase, owners still reported improvement of about 2 points, suggesting a caregiver expectation effect. The authors suggest that trials with unblinded owners should add an outcome assessed by someone who does not know the allocation."},{"title":"Owner adherence to calorie restriction plans for dogs: a prospective study in nine practices","authors":"Lachance-Obi R, Sundqvist-Mahlangu H, Ferris-Tanaka O","year":2023,"venue":"Companion Animal Practice Research","doi":"10.5555/capr.2023.0094","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 310 dogs started on a calorie restriction plan in nine first-opinion practices for six months. Owners reported following the daily food allowance on 81 percent of days in the first month and on 57 percent of days in the sixth month. Begging, scavenging or waking at night for food were reported by 34 percent of owners, and these dogs lost less weight. Households with children or several adults feeding the dog had lower adherence. The authors recommend asking about hunger behaviours at every visit."},{"title":"Pragmatic trials in companion animal practice: recruitment and retention across practice groups","authors":"Whitlock-Danso C, Imai-Fairfax B","year":2024,"venue":"Veterinary Research Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We summarised recruitment and retention in 14 pragmatic trials run in first-opinion practice groups. Median recruitment was 3.2 animals per practice per month, ranging from 0.8 to 6.1, and was highest where a named nurse or vet champion screened appointment lists. Median retention at six months was 78 percent. Trials that allocated animals centrally by a web system reported fewer protocol deviations than those using envelopes held in practices. Outcome assessment by a clinician unaware of allocation was reported in 6 of 14 trials."},{"title":"Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use during weight loss programmes in dogs with osteoarthritis","authors":"Bergstrom-Eze T, Calloway-Mori N","year":2019,"venue":"Veterinary Pharmacology and Therapeutics Notes","doi":"10.5555/vptn.2019.0310","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed prescribing records for 205 dogs with osteoarthritis enrolled in weight loss programmes at four practices. Among dogs that lost at least 10 percent of their starting weight, 29 percent had their non-steroidal anti-inflammatory dose reduced or stopped within six months, against 8 percent of dogs that lost less. Dose changes were made by the treating vet without a protocol, and some reductions may have reflected owner preference. The authors suggest recording analgesic use as an outcome in weight loss trials."}]}
